summary: A detailed analysis of the prohibition against slaughtering sacrifices outside the Temple. The Gemara refines the scope: the prohibition applies only to animals intended as sacrificial offerings, not to routine food slaughter. The same physical act is either a legitimate meal or a violation incurring kareth (spiritual excision) depending entirely on intent. The theological underpinning: the Temple is the exclusive intermediary for sacrificial worship; bypassing it is not just procedurally wrong but a fundamental violation of how the divine-human encounter through sacrifice is designed to work.

learning.ahaMoment: The prohibition is about intent: routine slaughter for food is permitted everywhere; only slaughtering with sacrificial intent outside the Temple violates the prohibition. Intent transforms the same physical act into either food or forbidden sacrifice.
learning.memoryAnchor: The same physical cut: but with sacrificial intent outside the Temple, it becomes kareth. Intent changes everything in Temple law.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does intentional slaughter of consecrated animals outside the Temple carry the severe penalty of kareth (spiritual excision), and what category of transgression does this represent?
learning.coreTension: Many Temple violations carry less severe penalties; the severity of kareth for outside slaughter suggests this is not merely a procedural error but a fundamental transgression - yet what makes bypassing the Temple's location requirement so grave?
learning.coreMove: The prohibition targets intentional sacrificial acts that bypass the Temple; kareth is the penalty because outside sacrifice is not a location error but an assertion of alternative sacred authority - it challenges the Temple's exclusive role as covenantal intermediary between Israel and God, making spiritual excision the structurally appropriate response.

takeaway.text: Intentional slaughter of consecrated animals outside the Temple carries kareth because it is not a procedural location error but an assertion of alternative sacred authority; bypassing the Temple's exclusive role as covenantal intermediary is a fundamental transgression of Israel's covenantal structure, warranting spiritual excision.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may view kareth for outside slaughter as a disproportionate penalty for a location violation; they miss that intentional outside sacrifice challenges the Temple's exclusive authority as covenantal intermediary, making it a fundamental transgression rather than a technical error.

quizSeeds.answer: Only when the animal is intended as a sacrifice (burnt-offering, sin-offering, etc.) and is slaughtered outside the Temple. Routine slaughter for food is not subject to this prohibition. The penalty for violation is kareth.

sugyot.finalRuling: The outside-slaughter prohibition requires sacrificial intent; routine food slaughter is permitted everywhere. Violation with sacrificial intent incurs kareth.

rashiTranslations.en: 'If [I understand] "offering" to mean,' etc. - the opening of the braita in Torat Kohanim states as follows:
one might think that one who slaughters non-sacred animals inside would be liable, and this could be derived by logical inference, etc.; the verse teaches, 'offering' - for an offering
is one liable, but not for a non-sacred animal. 'If [I understand] "offering" to mean,' etc. - meaning, or
does the word 'offering' come only to exclude non-sacred animals slaughtered inside, but rather to include consecrated property of the
Temple treasury slaughtered outside, that he should be liable, since
these too are called 'offering,' as in the verse that states,
'and we brought the offering of the Lord, whatever any man found' -
and this certainly refers to Temple-treasury property. 'Fit for
the entrance,' etc. - and Temple-treasury property was never
destined to come to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
But I have heard that they are not fit for the entrance of the Tent
of Meeting for a different reason: that ordinary Temple-treasury property consists of
blemished animals, for the master said (Temurah 7b)
that one who consecrates unblemished animals for Temple-treasury use transgresses
a positive commandment; and I cannot establish it that way in its proper place, as it should be understood in tractate
Zevachim. 'And I do not exclude the red heifer' -
we do not read it that way, reasoning that it too is not fit
to come to the Tent of Meeting; rather, the correct reading is 'and I do not exclude
the goat that is sent away,' which is fit to come to the Tent
of Meeting for the lottery and for the confession said over it. This is
how it is explained in Zevachim. 'And "to the Lord" comes to exclude'
regarding the goat that is sent away, which IS fit
to come? This is said in astonishment. 'These are the fire-offerings' - meaning he shall not place
any of it on the fire of the arrangement. 'From where do we know that one should not
consecrate it while it lacks its time? The verse teaches, "offering"' -
for from the moment of its consecration it is already called an offering. 'There,
in the first verse, "to the entrance" comes to include' - the goat that is sent away,
since it is not excluded by "to the entrance," for it is indeed fit
to come to the entrance. '"To the Lord" comes to exclude' -
since if it came to include, it would not be necessary; rather, since it comes
to exclude, it comes to teach: whatever is exclusively designated
for the Name is included, and this one, not exclusively designated, is excluded. 'Here,
in the second verse, "fire-offering" implies exclusion' - of the goat that is sent away,
since it is not offered up as a fire-offering. '"To the Lord" comes for inclusion' -
and it comes to teach: to the Lord, meaning anything that belongs to the Lord. 'But does not
the lottery designate' - for the Name only that which is fit
for the Name? And since one does not know upon which of the two
the lottery for the Name will fall, it is impossible for either
of them to be lacking its time. 'This follows Chanan the Egyptian' -
who holds that once the lottery has been cast and one
of the pair dies, no new lottery is needed; therefore, when the goat to be sent away dies
and he brings another without a new lottery, it was necessary
to derive from the verse that he may not bring one lacking
its time. 'Even blood' - of the inner goat
already in the cup, having already been slaughtered, if the goat to be sent away then dies,
he brings its replacement from the marketplace. 'And pairs it' - with the blood,
and sends it away. 'For he does not hold of rejection' - meaning he does not hold
that the blood becomes rejected on account of its partner having died, such that one would say the blood must be poured out, as
Rabbi Yehuda states in the Mishnah: if the one sent away dies, the blood must be poured out. 'Perhaps he brings a new pair and casts lots' -
and lets the surviving goat graze until the lot for the Name falls upon it, and atonement is achieved through the blood of the first goat;
and in any case he must bring two and cast lots; but still it is obvious that one lacking
its time may not be included, since the lottery designates only that which is fit for the Name. 'Ravina said' -
the verse regarding one lacking its time is necessary for a case such as this: the goat to be sent away became blemished after the lottery had already fallen
upon it, and he transferred its sanctity onto another animal; and this replacement does not need a new lottery, since it comes by force of the first one's own designation.
'And you shall not give a fire-offering from them,' etc. - this is written regarding blemished animals. 'Some of them' - an olive's-bulk's worth of them.
'Rava' - the comment is truncated here; it continues on 64a as 'Rava said,' explaining a further case in which the verse about one lacking its time is needed.
